title: Genetics
subject: Biology

cards.prompt: What is DNA? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: DNA is a nucleotide polymer whose sequence carries hereditary information in cellular organisms. Complementary antiparallel strands support templated copying, although inheritance also depends on cellular context and not every genomic sequence encodes a protein.
accepted_variants: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the principal cellular genetic material.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all DNA consists of protein-coding genes.

cards.prompt: What is Gene? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A gene is a genomic sequence contributing to a functional product such as an RNA or protein, interpreted with its regulatory and processing context. Gene boundaries and definitions can vary with the biological question.
required_concepts: Genomic unit contributing to a functional product.
major_error_concepts: Defining every gene as one uninterrupted protein-coding stretch.

cards.prompt: What is Allele? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An allele is a sequence variant at a specified genetic locus. An individual can carry different alleles on homologous copies, and a population may contain more than two alleles at that locus.
required_concepts: Alternative sequence state at a locus.
Population diversity can exceed two alleles.
accepted_variants: A variant form of a genetic locus.
major_error_concepts: Treating dominant and recessive as the only two possible alleles in every population.

cards.prompt: What is Locus? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A locus is a specified position or region in a genome. It identifies where an allele or other genetic feature is located, rather than describing the individual's allele state.
major_error_concepts: Equating locus with the particular allele occupying it.

cards.prompt: What is Genome? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A genome is the complete set of genetic material considered for an organism, cell, or biological entity. The scope should specify nuclear versus organellar genomes and whether one haploid set or all copies is meant.
required_concepts: Complete genetic-material set under a stated scope.
major_error_concepts: Using genome as a synonym for the expressed genes alone.

cards.prompt: What is Chromosome? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chromosome is an organized DNA-containing unit carrying many loci. In eukaryotes it includes chromatin; a replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids until they separate.
required_concepts: Replication changes chromatid count without immediately doubling chromosome count by the centromere convention.
major_error_concepts: Calling each sister chromatid a separate unreplicated chromosome before segregation under the usual counting convention.

cards.prompt: What is Chromatin? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Chromatin is the DNA-protein complex organizing eukaryotic chromosomes. Its packaging and chemical state influence accessibility and gene activity without necessarily changing the DNA sequence.
accepted_variants: The material of eukaryotic chromosome organization.
major_error_concepts: Treating chromatin changes as necessarily DNA-sequence mutations.

cards.prompt: What is Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A mutation is a change in genetic sequence relative to a reference or prior state. Its effects range from neutral to consequential and depend on location, molecular change, and biological context.
required_concepts: Effect is context-dependent, not inherently harmful.
accepted_variants: A new alteration in genetic information.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every mutation changes phenotype or is deleterious.

cards.prompt: What is Polymorphism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A polymorphism is the presence of multiple genetic variants in a population. Frequency thresholds are conventional in some uses, and common variants are not automatically harmless or functionally important.
required_concepts: Population variation at a locus or sequence feature.
major_error_concepts: Assuming polymorphism means biologically neutral by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Genotype? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genotype is the allele composition of an individual at a specified locus, set of loci, or genomic scope. It differs from the observable phenotype resulting from genotype, environment, and their interactions.
required_concepts: Allelic constitution at a stated scope.
accepted_variants: The genetic state of an individual.
major_error_concepts: Equating genotype with visible appearance alone.

cards.prompt: What is Phenotype? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phenotype is an observable or measurable trait of an organism or cell. It reflects genetic contributions, environment, development, and their interactions rather than a one-to-one decoding of genotype in every case.
required_concepts: Can depend on environment and development as well as genotype.
major_error_concepts: Assuming identical genotypes must have identical phenotypes in every environment.

cards.prompt: What is Dominance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dominance describes the relationship between alleles for a specified phenotype in a heterozygote. A dominant allele's associated phenotype is expressed in that comparison; dominance does not imply greater frequency, fitness, or molecular strength.
required_concepts: Heterozygote phenotype relation at a specified trait.
accepted_variants: The expressed allele-associated phenotype in a heterozygous comparison.
major_error_concepts: Calling an allele dominant because it is common.

cards.prompt: What is Recessiveness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A recessive allele's associated phenotype is masked in the relevant heterozygote comparison under complete dominance. It may be expressed when no dominant counterpart is present, as in a homozygote or appropriate hemizygote.
required_concepts: Phenotypic masking in the specified heterozygote.
Expression need not require two copies in a hemizygous context.
accepted_variants: The hidden phenotype in a complete-dominance heterozygote.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a recessive allele is not transcribed or has no biological activity by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Codominance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Codominance occurs when both allele-associated phenotypic contributions are distinguishable in a heterozygote. This differs from an intermediate blended phenotype.
accepted_variants: Simultaneous expression of distinguishable allelic phenotypes.
major_error_concepts: Defining codominance solely as an intermediate phenotype.

cards.prompt: What is Incomplete Dominance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Incomplete dominance occurs when the heterozygote phenotype is intermediate between the compared homozygotes for the measured trait. The alleles remain discrete hereditary variants rather than permanently blending.
accepted_variants: Partial dominance in the specified phenotype.
major_error_concepts: Claiming intermediate phenotype means the original alleles cannot reappear in offspring.

cards.prompt: What is Homozygous Genotype? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An individual is homozygous at a diploid locus when the two homologous copies carry the same allele. Homozygosity is locus-specific unless a broader scope is stated.
required_concepts: Same allele on both homologous copies.
major_error_concepts: Calling an individual homozygous at all loci because one locus is homozygous.

cards.prompt: What is Heterozygous Genotype? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An individual is heterozygous at a diploid locus when its homologous copies carry different alleles. The resulting phenotype depends on the alleles and trait being measured.
required_concepts: Different alleles at the same homologous locus.
major_error_concepts: Defining heterozygosity as having two different genes at different loci.

cards.prompt: What is Genetic Linkage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genetic linkage is the tendency of loci on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Recombination can separate linked alleles, and distant loci can show an observed recombination fraction near one-half.
required_concepts: Crossing over can separate linked alleles.
major_error_concepts: Assuming linked genes can never recombine.

cards.prompt: What is Recombination Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Recombination frequency is the fraction of scored offspring or gametes that are recombinant for the marker pair. It ranges up to one-half in standard two-point analysis and underestimates long genetic distances when multiple exchanges go undetected.
required_concepts: Recombinant fraction in the scored products.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a fraction above one-half as ordinary two-locus linkage evidence without questioning the model or scoring.

cards.prompt: What is Map Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: One map unit or centimorgan corresponds locally to about one percent recombination for short intervals. Genetic distance can exceed 50 centimorgans because it accounts for crossover events not all visible in a two-point recombinant fraction.
required_concepts: Map distance differs from raw recombination fraction over long intervals.
major_error_concepts: Claiming 1 cM always equals a fixed number of base pairs.

cards.prompt: What is Sequence and Heredity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: DNA sequence stores heritable information because copying and transmitting nucleotide order preserves information across cell divisions and generations. Sequence variation can be inherited without necessarily producing a detectable phenotype.
required_concepts: Heritable information resides in nucleotide order.
Inheritance and observable effect are separate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming only variants with visible effects are inherited.

cards.prompt: What is Synonymous Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A synonymous coding mutation changes a codon without changing its encoded amino acid under the relevant genetic code. It can still affect splicing, RNA stability, or translation and is not automatically functionally neutral.
major_error_concepts: Equating synonymous with guaranteed absence of biological effect.

cards.prompt: What is Missense Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A missense mutation changes a coding sequence so that a codon specifies a different amino acid. Its effect depends on the substitution and protein context.
required_concepts: Codon change alters one encoded amino-acid identity.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every missense variant abolishes protein function.

cards.prompt: What is Nonsense Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonsense mutation changes a coding codon into a termination codon. It can shorten translation and may trigger RNA surveillance; its actual effect depends on position and transcript context.
required_concepts: Truncation or transcript decay may result.
major_error_concepts: Calling every amino-acid substitution nonsense.

cards.prompt: What is Frameshift Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A frameshift mutation inserts or deletes coding nucleotides in a number not divisible by three, changing the downstream reading frame. It often alters many subsequent codons and can introduce a premature stop.
required_concepts: Coding insertion/deletion not a multiple of three.
major_error_concepts: Calling every three-nucleotide coding deletion a frameshift.

cards.prompt: What is Linkage and Assortment Ratios? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linked loci can produce offspring ratios different from independent assortment because parental allele combinations are transmitted more often than recombinant combinations when recombination is below one-half. Phase and recombination fraction determine the expected classes.
major_error_concepts: Applying an unlinked dihybrid ratio automatically to tightly linked loci.

cards.prompt: What is Recombination and Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes exchanges corresponding DNA segments and can create new combinations of alleles. This molecular exchange connects chromosome behavior in meiosis with observed recombinant inheritance.
required_concepts: Homologous DNA exchange generates recombinant combinations.
accepted_variants: The chromosome-level basis of recombination inheritance.
major_error_concepts: Attributing ordinary crossover recombination to swapping unrelated whole genes between arbitrary chromosomes.

cards.prompt: What is Complementation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A complementation test places two recessive mutations in the same cell or individual to ask whether functional copies together restore a phenotype. Restoration often indicates mutations in different genes; noncomplementation often indicates the same gene, with important exceptions.
required_concepts: Test functional restoration when recessive mutations are combined.
Same-gene inference is conditional, not absolute.
accepted_variants: A functional test of whether mutations affect the same complementation group.
major_error_concepts: Treating complementation as proof that two mutations are physically adjacent.

cards.prompt: What is Penetrance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a specified genotype who display its defined phenotype under the assessed conditions. Incomplete penetrance means some carriers do not show that phenotype.
required_concepts: Fraction of genotype carriers expressing the specified trait.
accepted_variants: Probability of phenotypic expression conditional on genotype and context.
major_error_concepts: Confusing penetrance with how severe the trait is among affected carriers.

cards.prompt: What is Expressivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Expressivity is the degree or pattern of phenotypic manifestation among individuals with a genotype. Variable expressivity concerns differences in manifestation rather than the fraction showing any phenotype.
accepted_variants: Variation in trait presentation among genotype carriers.
major_error_concepts: Using expressivity to mean the percentage of carriers affected.

cards.prompt: What is Pleiotropy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Pleiotropy occurs when one gene influences multiple traits. The effects can arise through a shared molecular role or a cascade of developmental and physiological consequences.
required_concepts: One gene affects multiple phenotypic traits.
accepted_variants: Multiple trait effects of one locus.
major_error_concepts: Confusing pleiotropy with many genes contributing to one trait.

cards.prompt: What is Epistasis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Epistasis is an interaction in which the phenotypic effect of one locus depends on genotype at another locus. In classical crosses, masking or modification can alter expected trait ratios.
major_error_concepts: Confusing epistasis with dominance between alleles at the same locus.

cards.prompt: What is Maternal Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A maternal-effect trait is influenced by the mother's genotype through products or conditions she supplies to the egg or early offspring. It is distinct from inheritance of mitochondrial DNA and from genomic imprinting.
required_concepts: Maternal genotype affects offspring phenotype through maternal contribution.
accepted_variants: Parental-effect inheritance through the egg environment or supplied products.
major_error_concepts: Calling every maternally transmitted mitochondrial trait a maternal-effect nuclear gene.

cards.prompt: What is Mitochondrial Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mitochondrial inheritance transmits variants in mitochondrial genomes, commonly through the maternal lineage in animals. Heteroplasmy and segregation of mitochondrial variants can produce variable expression; patterns vary across organisms.
required_concepts: Common maternal transmission with potential heteroplasmy.
major_error_concepts: Applying ordinary diploid Mendelian segregation ratios directly to mitochondrial heteroplasmy.

cards.prompt: What is Haploinsufficiency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Haploinsufficiency occurs when one functional copy of a gene does not provide enough activity for the usual phenotype. Loss of one copy can therefore produce a phenotype in a heterozygote.
accepted_variants: A dosage requirement exceeding one normal copy.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every heterozygous loss-of-function mutation is haploinsufficient.

cards.prompt: What is Dominant-Negative Allele? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A dominant-negative allele produces a product that interferes with the function of the normal product or its complex. Its effect is more than merely reducing the number of functional copies.
required_concepts: Mutant product disrupts normal function in the presence of wild-type product.
major_error_concepts: Equating dominant negative with any dominant phenotype or simple gene deletion.

cards.prompt: What is Gain-of-Function Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A gain-of-function mutation increases activity, creates a new activity, or changes the timing or location of activity. Dominance depends on the trait and mechanism, though many such alleles act in heterozygotes.
accepted_variants: A mutation adding or increasing a functional effect.
major_error_concepts: Calling every dominant mutation gain of function.

cards.prompt: What is Allele-Specific Measurements? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Allele-specific measurements compare signals assigned to distinct alleles, such as variant read counts. Interpretation must consider ploidy, mapping bias, copy number, sampling noise, and whether DNA or RNA was measured.
required_concepts: Technical and biological factors affect observed ratios.
accepted_variants: Allelic imbalance analysis with context-dependent interpretation.
major_error_concepts: Treating every unequal read count as proof of allele-specific expression.

cards.prompt: What is Conditional Allele? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conditional allele changes its functional effect depending on an imposed condition, such as temperature or tissue-specific recombination. It permits gene function to be perturbed in a chosen context rather than constitutively everywhere.
required_concepts: Allele effect depends on a specified condition.
major_error_concepts: Assuming conditional means the allele is never functional.

cards.prompt: What is Temperature-Sensitive Mutant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A temperature-sensitive mutant functions relatively normally at a permissive temperature but loses or changes function at a restrictive temperature. The experimental interpretation requires controls for temperature effects independent of the mutation.
major_error_concepts: Attributing every heat response to the mutant allele without controls.

cards.prompt: State Mendel's law of segregation and its ordinary transmission expectation. Does it imply that every organism produces gametes directly by meiosis?
cards.definition: At a diploid locus, the two allele copies segregate through meiosis into haploid lineages, so ordinary haploid gametes carry one allele at that locus. Equal transmission is expected absent segregation distortion. Gametes need not be direct meiotic products: in plants, meiosis produces spores and the haploid gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis.
required_concepts: Ordinary haploid gametes receive one allele at a locus; equal transmission assumes ordinary segregation without distortion.
Segregation through meiosis does not imply direct meiotic production of gametes in every life cycle.
accepted_variants: Alleles segregate into haploid lineages, with one allele transmitted per gamete; plant gametes can form mitotically after meiotic spore formation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming both homologous alleles normally enter every haploid gamete.
Claiming plant gametophytes must use meiosis to make gametes.

cards.prompt: What is Independent Assortment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Independent assortment means allele transmission at one locus is independent of transmission at another under the modeled cross. Unlinked loci, or loci with an observed recombination fraction of one-half, show the standard independent proportions.
required_concepts: Joint transmission factors into independent locus probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Applying independent assortment to every pair of loci on the same chromosome regardless of linkage.

cards.prompt: What is Meiosis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Meiosis uses one DNA replication followed by two divisions to reduce chromosome-set number. Homologous chromosomes segregate in meiosis I and sister chromatids ordinarily segregate in meiosis II, with recombination occurring during the first division's prophase.
accepted_variants: Reductional then equational division producing haploid products.
major_error_concepts: Claiming DNA is replicated again between meiosis I and II.

cards.prompt: What is Homologous Chromosomes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci in comparable order and usually come from the two parents in a diploid organism. They can carry different alleles and are not the same as replicated sister chromatids.
accepted_variants: The matched chromosome pair in a diploid set.
major_error_concepts: Assuming homologs are necessarily identical in DNA sequence.

cards.prompt: What is Sister Chromatids? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sister chromatids are replicated copies of one chromosome, initially closely matched in sequence and joined through centromere-associated cohesion. They separate during mitosis or meiosis II under the standard pattern.
required_concepts: Copies produced by replication of one chromosome.
accepted_variants: The paired chromatids of a replicated chromosome.
major_error_concepts: Calling the maternal and paternal homologs sister chromatids.

cards.prompt: What is Haploid? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Haploid describes one complete chromosome set, symbolized n. Chromosome replication doubles DNA content without by itself changing ploidy.
required_concepts: Ploidy differs from DNA replication state.
major_error_concepts: Calling a replicated haploid cell diploid solely because DNA amount doubled.

cards.prompt: What is Diploid? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Diploid describes two homologous chromosome sets, symbolized 2n. The term counts sets rather than chromatids or DNA mass.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every diploid cell has exactly two DNA molecules total.

cards.prompt: What is Fertilization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fertilization combines gametes and their genetic contributions to form a zygote. In the standard diploid sexual cycle, fusion of two haploid gametes restores diploidy.
required_concepts: Haploid plus haploid restores diploid in the standard cycle.
accepted_variants: Formation of the zygote through gamete fusion.
major_error_concepts: Confusing fertilization with chromosome replication.

cards.prompt: What is Crossing Over? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Crossing over is reciprocal exchange between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiotic recombination. It can create recombinant chromatids while helping establish connections important for homolog segregation.
major_error_concepts: Describing ordinary crossing over as exchange between sister chromatids only.

cards.prompt: What is Punnett Square? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Punnett square enumerates combinations of parental gametes to predict offspring genotype probabilities under specified transmission assumptions. It does not guarantee the exact counts in a small family.
required_concepts: Expected proportions differ from guaranteed sample counts.
accepted_variants: A table of possible fertilization combinations.
major_error_concepts: Treating a 1:4 probability as a requirement that exactly one of every four offspring shows the outcome.

cards.prompt: What is Testcross? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A testcross crosses an individual of uncertain genotype with an appropriate homozygous recessive tester. Offspring classes reveal the tested individual's gametes under the dominance and viability assumptions of the cross.
required_concepts: Use a recessive tester to expose gametic allele combinations.
accepted_variants: A diagnostic cross against a recessive genotype.
major_error_concepts: Calling every cross between two heterozygotes a testcross.

cards.prompt: What is Reciprocal Cross? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reciprocal crosses exchange which sex carries each parental genotype. Different outcomes can suggest sex linkage, cytoplasmic inheritance, or parental effects rather than an ordinary sex-independent autosomal model.
required_concepts: Reverse the sexes of genotype assignments.
Differences point to sex or parent-origin mechanisms.
accepted_variants: Paired crosses with maternal and paternal roles swapped.
major_error_concepts: Assuming reciprocal differences uniquely prove mitochondrial inheritance.

cards.prompt: What is Pedigree? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A pedigree charts biological relationships and a trait across generations. It supports inference about inheritance patterns, but small families, incomplete penetrance, and uncertain phenotyping can leave several models compatible.
major_error_concepts: Treating a small pedigree as definitive proof of a unique mode without considering penetrance.

cards.prompt: What is Autosomal Dominant Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Autosomal dominant inheritance involves a dominant trait associated with a non-sex-chromosome locus. Under a simple fully penetrant heterozygote-by-unaffected cross, each offspring has one-half probability of inheriting the allele, independent of sex.
required_concepts: One-half risk applies to the stated cross and assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every affected parent transmits the allele to every child.

cards.prompt: What is Autosomal Recessive Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires the relevant recessive genotype at an autosomal locus for the simple trait. Two heterozygous carriers yield expected genotype proportions 1:2:1 and a one-quarter affected fraction under complete penetrance and ordinary segregation.
required_concepts: Carrier cross proportions are conditional expectations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming unaffected parents cannot have an affected recessive offspring.

cards.prompt: What is X-Linked Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: X-linked inheritance concerns loci on the X chromosome. In the typical XX/XY system, XY individuals are hemizygous for most X-linked loci, and fathers transmit their X chromosome to daughters rather than sons.
required_concepts: Hemizygosity and sex-specific transmission in the stated system.
major_error_concepts: Inferring father-to-son X transmission in the standard XX/XY model.

cards.prompt: What is Y-Linked Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Y-linked inheritance concerns loci on the Y chromosome outside shared recombining regions. In the typical XX/XY system, such variants follow the paternal Y lineage to sons, subject to the locus and reproductive context.
required_concepts: Y-chromosome-specific transmission in the stated system.
accepted_variants: Holandric inheritance for a Y-specific locus.
major_error_concepts: Calling a trait Y-linked simply because it is observed only in males.

cards.prompt: What is Nondisjunction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nondisjunction is failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate correctly during division. It can generate cells or gametes with abnormal numbers of particular chromosomes.
required_concepts: Homologs or sisters can be involved at different divisions.
major_error_concepts: Equating nondisjunction with deletion of a small DNA segment.

cards.prompt: What is Aneuploidy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Aneuploidy is gain or loss of individual chromosomes rather than whole chromosome sets. Monosomy and trisomy are common examples of the category.
major_error_concepts: Calling a triploid whole-set genome aneuploid by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Polyploidy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polyploidy is the presence of more than two complete chromosome sets. It differs from aneuploidy and can arise through genome duplication or combination of chromosome sets from different lineages.
major_error_concepts: Calling one extra chromosome polyploidy.

cards.prompt: What is Chromosomal Deletion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chromosomal deletion removes a segment of DNA, potentially altering gene dosage or disrupting regulatory and coding regions. Its effects depend on the segment and genetic background.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a deletion always removes an entire chromosome.

cards.prompt: What is Chromosomal Duplication? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chromosomal duplication creates an additional copy of a genomic segment. It can change dosage and provide material for divergence, but consequences depend on the affected genes and context.
required_concepts: Extra copy of a genomic segment.
major_error_concepts: Equating duplication with whole-chromosome-set doubling in every case.

cards.prompt: What is Chromosomal Inversion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chromosomal inversion reverses the orientation of a segment within a chromosome. It can alter gene context and affect meiotic recombination outcomes in heterozygotes without necessarily changing total DNA dosage.
major_error_concepts: Defining inversion as exchange of material between two different chromosomes.

cards.prompt: What is Chromosomal Translocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chromosomal translocation moves or exchanges segments between chromosome locations, often different chromosomes. A balanced rearrangement can preserve overall dosage while still affecting genes or meiotic segregation.
required_concepts: Relocation or exchange of chromosome segments.
Balanced dosage does not guarantee no biological effect.
accepted_variants: An interchromosomal or relocated segment rearrangement.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every translocation necessarily changes total gene copy number.

cards.prompt: What is Copy-Number Variation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Copy-number variation is variation in the number of copies of a genomic segment among individuals or cells. Duplications and deletions can create it, and copy number can affect dosage and sequencing read ratios.
major_error_concepts: Treating a single-nucleotide substitution as a copy-number change.

cards.prompt: What is Coupling and Repulsion Phase? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coupling phase places two specified alleles on the same homolog, such as AB/ab; repulsion places them on opposite homologs, such as Ab/aB. Phase determines which gamete classes are parental in a linkage analysis.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring phase when assigning recombinant testcross offspring.

cards.prompt: What is Three-Point Mapping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Three-point mapping uses offspring classes at three linked loci to infer gene order and distances. Comparing parental and double-recombinant classes helps identify the middle locus, while distance estimates count relevant crossovers.
required_concepts: Three linked markers establish order and intervals.
Double exchanges must be accounted for.
major_error_concepts: Using only the rarest single class without checking viability, scoring, and parental phase.

cards.prompt: What is Crossover Interference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Crossover interference describes dependence between crossover events in neighboring intervals. A common estimate is one minus the coefficient of coincidence, where that coefficient is observed divided by expected double crossovers under the independence model.
required_concepts: Crossovers in nearby intervals are not necessarily independent.
Interference uses observed versus independently expected doubles.
accepted_variants: Modification of nearby crossover probability by another crossover.
major_error_concepts: Assuming interference must always be positive by definition.

cards.prompt: What is LOD Score? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A LOD score is a base-ten log likelihood ratio comparing a linkage model at a specified recombination fraction with an unlinked model. Positive values support the tested linkage model relative to the null, with interpretation depending on the study design and threshold convention.
required_concepts: Log10 likelihood ratio against an unlinked model.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a LOD value itself as the probability that loci are linked.

cards.prompt: What is Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium gives genotype proportions p squared, 2pq, and q squared for two alleles under random mating and the standard population assumptions. Stable allele frequencies additionally require negligible selection, mutation, migration, and drift.
required_concepts: Distinguish random-mating proportions from assumptions for unchanged frequencies across generations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming observed Hardy-Weinberg proportions prove no evolutionary force ever acts.

cards.prompt: What is Allele Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Allele frequency is the fraction of gene copies at a specified locus carrying a particular allele in the sampled population. Diploid individuals contribute two copies at an autosomal locus under the ordinary model.
required_concepts: Allele copies divided by all locus copies.
major_error_concepts: Using carrier frequency as allele frequency without accounting for homozygotes and heterozygotes.

cards.prompt: What is Genotype Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genotype frequency is the fraction of individuals or sampled cells with a specified genotype. At a diploid two-allele locus, the three genotype frequencies sum to one and jointly determine allele frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Assuming genotype and allele frequencies are interchangeable quantities.

cards.prompt: What is Genetic Drift? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies caused by finite sampling of transmitted gene copies. It is stronger in smaller effective populations and can fix or lose variants regardless of their adaptive value.
required_concepts: Strength depends on effective population size.
major_error_concepts: Defining drift as directed change toward fitter alleles.

cards.prompt: What is Natural Selection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Natural selection changes variant representation through differences in survival or reproductive contribution associated with heritable traits. Its outcome depends on environment, genetic relationships, and other evolutionary forces.
required_concepts: No foresight or guaranteed progress toward perfection.
accepted_variants: Differential reproductive success of heritable variants.
major_error_concepts: Claiming organisms mutate because they need an advantageous trait.

cards.prompt: What is Gene Flow? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gene flow moves alleles between populations through migration followed by reproduction or other transfer processes. It can alter allele frequencies and reduce differentiation, depending on direction and magnitude.
major_error_concepts: Equating movement of nonreproducing individuals with gene flow in every case.

cards.prompt: What is Inbreeding? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inbreeding is mating between relatives relative to the population baseline, increasing the chance that paired alleles are identical by descent. It commonly raises homozygosity without by itself requiring an immediate change in allele frequencies.
required_concepts: Increased shared ancestry of paired alleles.
Genotype proportions can change without corresponding allele-frequency change.
accepted_variants: Mating that increases identity by descent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming inbreeding necessarily creates new deleterious mutations.

cards.prompt: What is Broad-Sense Heritability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Broad-sense heritability H squared is the proportion of phenotypic variance attributed to total genetic variance in a specified population and environment. It is not the fraction of an individual's trait caused by genes.
required_concepts: Context-specific, not an individual causal fraction.
accepted_variants: Total genetic contribution to observed trait variance.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting high heritability as proof that environment cannot change the trait.

cards.prompt: What is Narrow-Sense Heritability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Narrow-sense heritability h squared is additive genetic variance divided by phenotypic variance in the specified setting. It relates to predictable parent-offspring resemblance and simple selection-response approximations under their assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Including all dominance and interaction variance in the numerator by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Polygenic Trait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A polygenic trait receives contributions from multiple loci. It may vary continuously, but the phenotype also depends on effect sizes, interactions, and environment rather than gene count alone.
major_error_concepts: Confusing polygenic inheritance with pleiotropy of one gene.

cards.prompt: What is Quantitative Trait Locus? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A quantitative trait locus is a genomic region statistically associated with variation in a quantitative trait. A mapped region may contain multiple genes and is not automatically the exact causal variant.
required_concepts: Genomic region linked to quantitative variation.
Resolution and causality remain separate questions.
accepted_variants: A QTL interval influencing or associated with trait variation.
major_error_concepts: Treating a broad mapping interval as one proven causal nucleotide.

cards.prompt: What is Genome-Wide Association Study? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A genome-wide association study tests associations between genetic variants and phenotypes across the genome. Population structure, multiple testing, and linkage disequilibrium affect interpretation; association alone does not establish the causal variant or mechanism.
required_concepts: Association, confounding, and causality must be distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Calling every associated marker the directly causal mutation.

cards.prompt: What is Genomic Imprinting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genomic imprinting produces parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression through inherited epigenetic states that are reset in the germline according to the relevant developmental program. It differs from a maternal-effect genotype acting through egg contents.
required_concepts: Epigenetic state rather than a required DNA-sequence difference.
major_error_concepts: Equating imprinting with all maternally inherited traits.

cards.prompt: What is Sex-Limited Trait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sex-limited trait is expressed in only one sex under the relevant biology even though the underlying alleles may be carried by both. The causal loci need not be on sex chromosomes.
accepted_variants: A trait whose phenotypic expression is sex-restricted.
major_error_concepts: Inferring Y linkage simply because a trait appears only in males.

cards.prompt: What is Sex-Influenced Trait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sex-influenced trait has expression or dominance relationships that differ between sexes because of physiological context. It can be autosomal and is not defined by chromosome location.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sex-influenced trait must be located on the X chromosome.

cards.prompt: What is Sex Linkage versus Autosomal Inheritance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sex linkage refers to a locus's location on a sex chromosome, whereas autosomal inheritance refers to a non-sex chromosome. Sex-biased expression alone does not determine which location applies.
required_concepts: Expression bias does not establish location.
major_error_concepts: Classifying every sex-specific phenotype as sex-linked.

cards.prompt: What is Mutagen? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A mutagen is an agent that increases the rate of genetic mutations, often by causing DNA damage or interfering with replication or repair. Not every damaging exposure necessarily leaves a fixed mutation.
required_concepts: Damage and fixed mutation are different states.
accepted_variants: A mutation-promoting physical or chemical agent.
major_error_concepts: Equating every temporary DNA lesion with an inherited mutation.

cards.prompt: What is DNA Repair? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: DNA repair comprises processes that recognize and correct DNA damage or replication errors. Different pathways address different lesions, and repair can be accurate or mutagenic depending on the mechanism and template availability.
required_concepts: Correction or processing of DNA damage and errors.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all repair is error-free or that all lesions use the same pathway.

cards.prompt: What is Germline versus Somatic Mutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Germline mutations occur in cells contributing genetic material to offspring and can be transmitted across generations. Somatic mutations occur in other body-cell lineages and are generally not transmitted through gametes, though they can expand within tissues.
required_concepts: Distinguish reproductive lineage from body-cell lineage.
Somatic variants may be clonally propagated within an individual.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every mutation detected in a body sample is present in all gametes.

cards.prompt: What is Gene–Environment Interaction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A gene-environment interaction occurs when a genotype's phenotypic effect differs across environments. It is more than simply separate additive genetic and environmental contributions.
major_error_concepts: Calling every trait influenced independently by genes and environment an interaction without effect dependence.

cards.prompt: What is Complementation versus Epistasis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Complementation tests whether two mutations can supply each other's missing functions, often informing same-gene versus different-gene grouping. Epistasis examines how genotypes at different loci modify a combined phenotype; the tests answer different questions.
required_concepts: Functional restoration versus between-locus phenotypic interaction.
accepted_variants: Distinguishing complementation-group analysis from pathway or genetic-interaction analysis.
major_error_concepts: Treating noncomplementation and epistasis as identical evidence of one mechanism.

cards.prompt: What is Replica Plating? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Replica plating transfers colonies in a matching spatial pattern to different media, allowing growth phenotypes to be compared and original colonies recovered. It can demonstrate that resistant variants existed before exposure in the classic experimental logic.
required_concepts: Growth comparisons distinguish preexisting variants from selection during exposure under the design.
major_error_concepts: Concluding selection directed the required mutation merely because resistant colonies survive.

cards.prompt: What is Tetrad Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Tetrad analysis examines all products of a single meiosis, as in suitable fungi, to study segregation and recombination. Ordered and unordered tetrads provide different information about crossover position and gene-centromere relationships.
required_concepts: Analyze the full meiotic product set.
accepted_variants: Genetic analysis of individual meiotic tetrads.
major_error_concepts: Treating unrelated offspring pooled from many meioses as one tetrad.

cards.prompt: What is Linkage Disequilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linkage disequilibrium is nonrandom association of alleles at different loci in a population. It can reflect physical linkage, population history, selection, or structure and does not require the loci to be adjacent or even linked physically.
required_concepts: Population allelic association departs from independent frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Assuming linkage disequilibrium proves close physical proximity.

cards.prompt: What is Genetic versus Physical Map? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A genetic map measures recombination-based distance, usually in centimorgans, while a physical map measures genomic position or base-pair distance. Their relationship varies because recombination rates are not uniform across the genome.
major_error_concepts: Applying one universal base-pairs-per-centimorgan conversion to every region.

cards.prompt: What is Recombination Hotspot? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A recombination hotspot is a genomic region with elevated recombination frequency relative to its surroundings in the relevant organism and context. Hotspots make genetic and physical distances nonuniformly related.
major_error_concepts: Assuming crossovers are uniformly distributed along physical DNA length.

cards.prompt: What is Balanced Rearrangement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A balanced chromosomal rearrangement preserves overall copy number of the rearranged material. It may still disrupt genes, regulatory context, or meiotic segregation and therefore is not synonymous with no functional consequences.
required_concepts: No net dosage gain or loss in the rearranged material.
Functional and reproductive effects can remain.
major_error_concepts: Calling every balanced rearrangement harmless by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Genetic Mosaicism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Genetic mosaicism is the presence of genetically distinct cell populations within an individual derived from one zygote. Postzygotic mutation or chromosome changes can generate tissue-restricted variants.
required_concepts: Different genotypes among cells from one zygote.
major_error_concepts: Equating mosaicism with chimerism from genetically distinct zygotes.

cards.prompt: What is Sex Determination? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sex determination is the biological process establishing sexual developmental pathways. Mechanisms differ among organisms and can involve chromosome combinations, specific genes, dosage, or environmental signals; one mammalian scheme is not universal.
required_concepts: Developmental determination mechanism varies across organisms.
accepted_variants: The system specifying sexual developmental fate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all organisms use the same XX/XY determination mechanism.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Genetics.
